reviews.one_line_contribution: That the harm of failure-derived agent memory is carried by verbatim erroneous action content rather than by failure information per se — cross-episode retrieved failure items make an agent re-commit the flagged error class in proportion to how many erroneous steps they quote, and a positive rewrite of the corrected procedure keeps the corrective value while removing the drag — yielding a write-time rule that is free at read time.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Contextual Drag (arXiv:2602.04288, verified via s2cli/Semantic Scholar: 'the presence of failed attempts in the context biases subsequent generations toward structurally similar errors from the context') already owns the mechanism and the structural-similarity metric; this proposal's delta is the delivery channel (retrieved cross-episode memory instead of in-task attempts) and the framing/dose manipulation, which 2602.04288 does not run. Two further threats. (a) Honest Lying: Understanding Memory Confabulation in Reflexive Agents (arXiv:2605.29463, verified via s2cli/HF, 2026-05-31) already measures a 'Reflection Repetition Rate' showing that stored self-generated reflections produce persistent repeated errors across environment resets — that is the proposal's P1/P5 (failure-derived memory raises error recurrence across episodes) in an adjacent setting, and it is absent from the proposal's Related Work and its Collision Check; it does not vary framing, so it does not kill P2/P3, but it takes much of the 'cross-episode drag exists' novelty. (b) Experience Memory Graph (arXiv:2607.13884, verified) and Mistake Notebook Learning (arXiv:2512.11485, verified) both already store abstracted corrective guidance rather than raw failed steps, so the proposal's prescriptive payload ('write the correction, not the mistake') is close to current practice; the contribution is the controlled attribution, not the recommendation. Working against the proposal's direction: Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs (arXiv:2605.12978, verified) finds LLM-consolidated/rewritten memory degrades relative to preserved raw trajectories — a published result in tension with P4's F3 >= F4 > none ordering that the proposal does not engage.
reviews.strongest_objection: F1 and F3 are not content-matched in the way the framing claim requires: F1 puts erroneous action strings in the context, F3 puts corrected action strings there. So the predicted ordering is the conjunction of two already-published effects — errors in context are imitated (2602.04288) and correct actions in context are imitated (few-shot demonstration) — and 'framing' is a re-description of which strings were pasted, not a new causal variable. This bites hardest on P4: on ALFWorld's tiny action space, a corrected procedure derived from a same-family failure and retrieved by task-description similarity is close to the solution for the current task, so F3's success advantage can be pure leakage rather than drag removal, and the instruction-only control (a generic 'verify preconditions' rule) is far too weak to absorb it. A second, independent objection: the primary metric is confounded with the secondary one. E1 (repeat re-opening) and E5 (invalid action) fire mechanically more often in longer, flailing episodes, so any condition that lowers success inflates the measured 'reproduction rate' without any imitation. Reproduction rate is not conditioned on failure, not step-normalized, and no per-step hazard is reported, so P1 and P3 can come out positive from the success drop alone — exactly the direction the hypothesis predicts, which makes the confirmatory result uninformative. Third, the framings are written by the same 27B model that acts and audited for content equivalence by a second local model with disagreements dropped: that drops items on the very axis under test and biases the bank toward phrasings both models find canonical.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: (1) Break the leakage explanation for P4 by adding a specificity-matched positive control: a corrected procedure for the same error class but a different object/receptacle family (the proposal already has this relevance control for F1 — apply it to F3), plus an F3 variant with target entities abstracted out. If F3's success gain survives entity abstraction and dies with relevance, the effect is about framing; if it tracks entity overlap, it is retrieval leakage. (2) Make the primary metric independent of success: report error-class recurrence as a per-step hazard, conditioned on failure and step-matched against the no-memory arm, with the null replicate estimating the hazard floor per class; keep the edit-distance structural-imitation measure as co-primary rather than secondary, since it is the metric that cannot be produced by longer episodes alone. (3) Add a condition that reproduces a published failure-memory pipeline as published, so the headline claim ('the benefit reported for failure memory depends on framing') is tested against something that actually reported a benefit. (4) Cite and differentiate arXiv:2605.29463 and arXiv:2605.12978 — the first pre-empts part of P1/P5, the second predicts the opposite sign for rewrites. (5) Have a third model, not one of the two used to generate and act, adjudicate content equivalence, and report the drop rate per framing so the selection is auditable. (6) Pre-register the applicability rule and the minimum stratum counts numerically; 'pre-registered minimum stratum counts' with no number is not a pre-registration.
reviews.missing_baseline: A published failure-memory method run as published — ExpeL's insight set or Mistake Notebook Learning's batch-clustered notes (arXiv:2512.11485), built from the same 800-task training stream and injected at the same k and token budget. The central claim is about 'the benefit reported for failure memory', but conditions F1-F4 are all the authors' own synthetic framings; without the real system in the design, a null or a reversal says nothing about the literature it is arguing with. Secondary omission: a leakage control for F3 (corrected procedure from a different object family, or with entities abstracted) — S, a full success trajectory, differs from F3 in abstraction level as well as provenance and therefore does not isolate it.

IDs the proposal leans on that I did NOT independently verify: 2607.12747, 2607.00685, 2607.01935, 2605.03354, 2606.22030, 2606.28450, 2605.17467, 2509.24088, 2607.01071, 2604.27003, 2605.18421, 2603.10600, 2601.11653 (several of these appear only in the automated novelty card or the proposal's own text). Judging the proposal's Collision Check itself: it is above average for this pipeline — it names channels, exact query strings, returned IDs, and honestly reports that its WebSearch budget was exhausted, and its central negative finding (no paper varies the framing of cross-episode failure memory) survived my seven independent queries. Two deductions: it missed arXiv:2605.29463, which already measures cross-episode error repetition from stored failure-derived reflections and is the nearest published measurement of its P1/P5, and it missed arXiv:2605.12978, which reports the opposite sign for LLM-rewritten memory versus raw trajectories and therefore threatens P4. A collision check that finds no competitor for its own hypothesis but also misses the two papers that most constrain its predicted directions has searched for the wrong thing in one direction.

reviews.one_line_contribution: That the harm of failure-derived agent memory is a property of how the item is written rather than of failure information per se: verbatim erroneous actions retrieved from other episodes induce a dose-dependent reproduction of the same error class during task execution, negation notes sit in between, and a positive rewrite of the corrected procedure retains the corrective value without the drag -- i.e. contextual drag extended from in-task context to cross-episode retrieved memory, with framing as the manipulated variable.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Two verified papers together cover most of the ground. (a) Contextual Drag, arXiv:2602.04288 (verified via s2cli/Semantic Scholar: 'the presence of failed attempts in the context biases subsequent generations toward structurally similar errors from the context'). It already establishes the mechanism, the structural-similarity metric, and the persistence under feedback/self-verification; the proposal's contribution reduces to a change of delivery channel (retrieved cross-episode item instead of in-task attempt) plus a framing factor. Scope extensions of a named published effect are the weakest kind of novelty at ICLR. (b) Honest Lying: Understanding Memory Confabulation in Reflexive Agents, arXiv:2605.29463 (verified via s2cli/Semantic Scholar; NOT cited by the proposal and NOT in its collision check). It is on ALFWorld, defines a Reflection Repetition Rate for the agent re-committing the stored error, shows that reflective memory reinforces rather than corrects failure, and -- critically -- its mitigation is precisely a rewrite of how the failure note is produced (replacing open-ended self-diagnosis with programmatic extraction of trajectory-level failure signals), reporting RRR 0.64 -> 0.10. That is the same benchmark, the same primary metric family (error repetition from a stored failure note), and the same shape of fix (change the note's construction, not the retrieval). It does not run the F1/F2/F3/F4 content-matched framing factorial and does not do a dose sweep, so it is not a full collision, but a reviewer who finds it will say the headline ('rewrite the failure note and the repetition goes away, on ALFWorld') is already demonstrated with a larger effect than this proposal is likely to measure. Also adjacent and verified: Experience Memory Graph, arXiv:2607.13884 (correction patterns from failed + expert trajectories -- the F3 form, already deployed as a method), Mistake Notebook Learning, arXiv:2512.11485 (distilled notes, not verbatim failures), and Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated by LLMs, arXiv:2605.12978 (verified; same trajectories yield qualitatively different memories under different write schedules, with an episodic-only control competitive with consolidation -- the write-path-decides-value thesis in a different guise, also uncited).
reviews.strongest_objection: The framings are not content-matched in the way the central claim requires, so the predicted ordering has a trivial explanation. F3 (positive rewrite of the corrected procedure) contains the correct action sequence; F1 (verbatim failed excerpt with a FAILED label) does not. Token-matching and filler padding equalize length, not information: F3 tells the agent what to do, F1 tells it only what someone else did wrong. If the result is F1 worst / F3 best, the paper will have shown that procedural instructions beat error exemplars -- which is not a framing effect and is not new -- and the abstract's claim that 'the benefit of failure memory depends on framing rather than on the presence of failure information' will not follow. The only genuinely matched contrast is F2 vs F3 (the same rule stated as a prohibition or as a prescription), and that is exactly the comparison the proposal's own P2 flags as its falsifier. In ALFWorld's small, templated action space that difference is plausibly a few points and lands inside this program's stated 0.05-0.14 run-to-run noise band, at which point the submission is a null on its own decisive test with a large confounded ordering around it. A second, related problem: 'tasks where the error class is applicable' does the heavy lifting in P1 and P4 but is never given a deterministic definition, and applicability correlates with the task family that similarity retrieval selects on, so the primary metric is computed on a post-hoc subset. Finally the budget arithmetic does not close: 6 conditions x 500 tasks x 3 seeds is 9k episodes for one backbone, and the plan lists three backbones plus a dose sweep and eight ablations, so the stated 'about 12k episodes' understates the real cost by roughly a factor of three to four.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Make F2 vs F3 the headline, not a cell in an ordering. (1) Pre-register the F2/F3 contrast as the confirmatory test, power it against the null replicate, and demote F1/F4 to descriptive context -- the honest claim is 'prohibition vs prescription at identical propositional content', not 'framing beats failure'. (2) Add the information-content control the design currently lacks: an F3-shaped positive procedure derived from a *success* trajectory of the same family (same corrected procedure, no failure provenance). If F3-from-failure equals F3-from-success, the failure content contributes nothing and the paper's real finding is that failure provenance is inert -- a cleaner and more interesting claim than the one proposed. (3) Add an error-class-tag-only item ('this family often fails by acting on a closed receptacle', no actions, no procedure) to bound how much of the effect survives when all erroneous content is removed, which is also the natural zero-dose point of the dose sweep. (4) Give a deterministic, pre-registered applicability rule per error class computed from the task specification before any rollout. (5) Cite and position against arXiv:2605.29463 and arXiv:2605.12978, and run at least one published failure-memory system (ExpeL avoid-style insights or Mistake Notebook Learning notes) in its native form as a condition, so F1-F4 are not four items the authors wrote themselves. (6) State the expected base rate of each error class under the no-memory condition from pilot data; a 1.5x multiplier on E1 loops may be unreachable by ceiling.
reviews.missing_baseline: A positive rewrite derived from a successful trajectory rather than from a failure (same corrected procedure, no failure provenance). Without it, F3's win cannot be attributed to 'rewriting the failure' as opposed to 'giving procedural guidance', and the paper cannot claim the failure content carries any value at all. Secondary omissions a reviewer will also demand: an error-class-tag-only item with zero erroneous content (the true zero dose), and at least one published failure-memory method (ExpeL insights or Mistake Notebook Learning notes) run natively rather than four author-written framings.

ID verification (s2cli paper): 2602.04288 VERIFIED (Contextual Drag, S2, 4 citations, matches the proposal's description), 2512.11485 VERIFIED (Mistake Notebook Learning, ACL, as described), 2605.08563 VERIFIED (Why Retrying Fails, context contamination on retry), 2606.31270 VERIFIED (Learning from Failure for computer-use agents), 2607.13884 VERIFIED (Experience Memory Graph), 2605.24941 VERIFIED (Memory-Induced Tool-Drift, personality bias, correctly set aside). Every ID the novelty argument leans on is real and described accurately, which is better than most submissions and I credit it. The hole: the check missed 2605.29463 (Honest Lying), which is on the proposal's own benchmark, defines a repetition-rate metric for a stored failure re-committed by the agent, and fixes it by changing how the note is written -- the single closest published result -- and 2605.12978 (Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated), which is the write-path-decides-value thesis at consolidation level and appears on the proposal's own novelty card at sim 0.59, unaddressed. Two of the card's top-five entries (2605.12978, 2607.13884) are given only a passing clause or none. So: a thorough, honest, well-instrumented check that nonetheless failed to surface the nearest neighbour, and the novelty score reflects what I verified rather than the check's confident closing sentence.

reviews.one_line_contribution: That failure-derived memory retrieved from *other* episodes makes an ALFWorld agent re-commit the specific error class it read about, at a rate that rises with the number of verbatim erroneous actions in the item at fixed tokens, and that rewriting the same lesson as a positive corrected procedure keeps the corrective value while removing the imitation — i.e. the value of failure memory sits in write-time framing, not in the presence of failure information.
reviews.closest_prior_work: VERIFIED via s2cli (Semantic Scholar): 'Honest Lying: Understanding Memory Confabulation in Reflexive Agents', arXiv:2605.29463 (2026-05-28). Same benchmark (ALFWorld), same phenomenon family, and essentially the same primary metric: it introduces a Reflection Repetition Rate for how often a stored failure-derived reflection's error recurs, reports RRR 0.64 for open-ended self-diagnosis, and concludes that 'reflective memory can reinforce false beliefs rather than correct them'. Critically, its mitigation is a *rewrite of how the note is written* — replacing open-ended self-diagnosis with programmatic extraction of trajectory-level failure signals — which drops RRR to 0.10 and solves 3 of 16 frozen environments. That is the proposal's headline finding (failure memory reproduces the flagged error; changing how the note is written removes it) already demonstrated on the proposal's own benchmark, three months before the proposal, and it is not cited. What survives: 2605.29463 uses self-generated, same-task reflective memory rather than cross-episode retrieval from a stranger's failure, it does not run a content-matched framing factorial (verbatim / negation / positive / contrastive), and it has no dose sweep over verbatim erroneous steps. So the proposal is not fully scooped, but its contribution shrinks to 'the rewrite axis is polarity, and the dose is verbatim error content' rather than 'failure memory drags and rewriting fixes it'. Secondary threats, both verified: Contextual Drag arXiv:2602.04288 (2026-02-04, verified — errors in context produce structurally similar errors across 11 models, mitigations fail) already owns the mechanism in-task; Experience Memory Graph arXiv:2607.13884 (2026-07-15, verified) already builds the positive-corrective form from failed + expert trajectories. From the older in-context-learning line, verified via s2cli: Contrastive Chain-of-Thought arXiv:2311.09277 and 'LLMs can implicitly learn from mistakes in-context' arXiv:2502.08550 both report that invalid/incorrect exemplars in context *help*, and 'Overthinking the Truth' arXiv:2307.09476 gives the false-induction-head account of harmful imitation from bad demonstrations — meaning both directions of the proposal's predicted ordering already have published support in the exemplar setting, and F4 (contrastive) is a rename of a 2023 method.
reviews.strongest_objection: Every cell of the predicted ordering is over-determined by two effects that are already established, so no outcome uniquely supports the proposal's causal story, and the one contrast that carries the title is confounded. (a) F1 > none is the expected consequence of in-context copying / false induction heads (arXiv:2307.09476) and of Contextual Drag itself (arXiv:2602.04288); demonstrating it cross-episode is a venue change, not a mechanism. (b) F2 > F3 is exactly what the long-standing negation-comprehension deficit predicts: 'do not X before Y' is harder to follow than 'do Y before X' whether or not any drag exists, and the proposal has no control that separates negation *comprehension* from error *imitation* (e.g. a negation note about an error class with no verbatim command strings versus a positive note with the same content — the plan's action-type paraphrase ablation touches this but is listed only under F2, not run as a factor). (c) The F1-versus-F3 contrast, which carries the abstract's claim that 'the benefit depends on framing rather than on the presence of failure information', is not a framing contrast at all: F1 (verbatim failed excerpt with a FAILED label) contains no statement of the correct action, while F3 (corrected procedure only) does. F3 > F1 is therefore fully explained by F3 containing the answer and F1 not containing it. The stated content-equivalence audit ('same error class, same correction') is internally inconsistent, since F1 by construction has no correction and cannot pass it. Token-matching and neutral filler equalise length, not information. A reviewer will say the study measures 'items that state the right action beat items that do not', which nobody disputes.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Three changes, in order of importance. (1) Run the actual 2x2 the title claims: polarity (negation versus positive) crossed with verbatim-error presence (item quotes the erroneous command strings versus does not), with corrective content held identical in all four cells. That means adding the missing cell — a positively framed item that still quotes the erroneous actions ('the agent did take X before opening Y; the correct step is to open Y first') — and its mirror, a negation note with the prohibition stated only at the action-type level. Only that design can attribute the effect to framing rather than to information content, and only it makes 'the note is the dose' a measurable coefficient rather than a slogan. (2) Position explicitly against arXiv:2605.29463: adopt or subsume its Reflection Repetition Rate, replicate its programmatic-extraction condition as a baseline framing, and state what the framing factorial adds beyond 'a better-written note has lower RRR'. Without this the paper reads as an unacknowledged re-derivation on the same benchmark. (3) Make the claim about *reported benefits* testable: the abstract asserts that 'the benefit reported for failure memory depends on framing', but no published failure-memory system is ever run. Take one system that reports a gain from failure memory (Mistake Notebook arXiv:2512.11485, ExpeL's avoid-style insights, or Reflexion) and swap only the framing of its stored items on the same pool, reporting whether its headline delta moves. That converts a phrasing study into an overturned result, which is what this track's Q8 asks for. Also add a negation-comprehension control and drop or rename F4, which is Contrastive CoT (arXiv:2311.09277) applied to traces.
reviews.missing_baseline: The positive-framed item that still contains the verbatim erroneous actions — the fourth cell of the polarity x verbatim-content 2x2. As written the plan has verbatim-plus-negative (F1), abstract-negative (F2), abstract-positive (F3) and F1+F3 concatenated (F4), so verbatim-error presence and negative polarity are perfectly confounded and the dose sweep exists only inside the negatively framed cell. A second omission a reviewer will demand: a matched-success trajectory that *contains the risky step handled correctly* (the plan's S is a generic same-family success, so S versus F1 compares 'no error present' with 'error present' rather than isolating how the same step is presented). Third, no published failure-memory system is run in any condition, so the claim about reported benefits has no baseline at all.
reviews.preprint_collision: No verified collision on the exact framing-dose claim, but the check is incomplete in a way that inflates the novelty argument, and it is not neutral. IDs verified with s2cli paper lookup: 2602.04288 confirmed (Contextual Drag, 2026-02-04); 2605.08563 confirmed (Why Retrying Fails, CCRM, 2026-05-08); 2606.31270 confirmed (Learning from Failure for computer-use agents, 2026-06-30); 2607.13884 confirmed (Experience Memory Graph, 2026-07-15); 2512.11485 confirmed (Mistake Notebook, 2025-12-12); 2605.18421 confirmed (EvoMemBench); 2512.16962 confirmed (MemoryGraft, 57 citations). Not independently verified in this session: 2605.24941, 2602.02475, 2606.00765, 2607.12747, 2509.25370, 2607.00685, 2607.01935 — these appeared in the automated card or the proposal's own text but I did not run paper lookups on them; none is load-bearing for my assessment. Judgement of the proposal's check: it is more specific than most (named IDs, two channels, honest about exhausting its WebSearch budget, and it correctly rules 2605.24941 out of scope), but it missed the single closest paper, arXiv:2605.29463, which is on ALFWorld, measures failure-derived reflective memory reproducing its own error at 0.64, and fixes it by changing how the note is written — despite the proposal running three ALFWorld-and-failure-memory queries. It also missed the negative-exemplar ICL line (2311.09277, 2502.08550, 2307.09476) that bears directly on F4 and on which direction the ordering should go, and MemoryGraft (2512.16962) on imitation from retrieved cross-episode items. A collision check that misses the nearest same-benchmark neighbour has not established novelty for the claim it is defending.
